passages.section: Gandhari's grief and her reproach to Krishna
passages.speaker: Gandhari
events: Gandhari surveys the dead
She holds Krishna accountable for allowing it
passages.summary: After the war, a woman who has lost all hundred sons tells the being who could have prevented it that he is answerable. Krishna accepts the reproach without silencing her. The text allows the charge to be made against a figure it otherwise treats as wise, and does not editorialise it away.
passages.source_reference: Stri Parva — Gandhari's reproach to Krishna
passages.verification_note: Episode identity verified against the standard 18-parva division; `summary` is an editorial rendering, not a quotation.

passages.speaker: Gandhari, Kunti and the women
events: The survivors walk among the dead
Each names her own loss
passages.summary: The chapter that follows the fighting is given over almost entirely to lament, including a quarrel about who has lost the most. The epic refuses to move quickly past the cost, and it gives equal weight to the mothers on the defeated side.
passages.source_reference: Stri Parva — the lamentations on the battlefield
passages.verification_note: Episode identity verified against the standard 18-parva division; `summary` is an editorial rendering, not a quotation.

passages.speaker: Krishna / Bhishma
events: Yudhishthira refuses the throne he has won
He is talked back into ruling
keywords: yudhishthira does not want to rule
passages.summary: Having won, the king does not want the kingdom. He is told that grief has its place and that duty continues afterwards. The passage separates two things people often conflate: the rightness of mourning, and the question of what you do on the following morning.
passages.source_reference: Shanti Parva — Yudhishthira's grief and return to duty
passages.verification_note: Episode identity verified against the standard 18-parva division; `summary` is an editorial rendering, not a quotation.

passages.section: Vidura Niti — the counsel to Dhritarashtra
passages.speaker: Vidura
events: Vidura sets out how a person in a position of responsibility should act
He describes the traits that ruin a ruler
passages.summary: A long discourse on conduct: how a person with authority should treat those beneath them, which appetites destroy judgement, and why a ruler who cannot hear bad news stops being able to act. Vidura's method is plain speech with worked consequences rather than exhortation.
passages.verification_note: Section identity (Vidura Niti within the Shanti Parva) verified; no chapter number is given because numbering differs across editions.

passages.section: Bhishma's discourse on dharma to Yudhishthira
passages.speaker: Bhishma
events: Yudhishthira asks questions about duty
Bhishma answers in a long discourse
passages.summary: Wounded and waiting, Bhishma becomes the epic's principal teacher. Yudhishthira asks concrete questions — about anger, about truth, about what a ruler owes a subject — and the answers are argued through cases rather than issued as slogans. The teaching comes from the man whose own commitments produced the disaster.
passages.source_reference: Shanti Parva — Bhishma's teaching on dharma
passages.verification_note: Section identity verified; the discourse continues into the Anushasana Parva and numbering differs across editions, so no chapter number is given.

passages.speaker: Bhishma
events: Bhishma gives detailed instructions on conduct and governance
He then prepares to leave his body
passages.summary: The last teaching concentrates on ordinary obligations: how wealth should be held, how speech should be used, what a person in charge owes to those who cannot leave. It is deliberately unglamorous, and it comes from the one figure in the war whose personal record was broadly acknowledged as clean.
passages.verification_note: Episode identity verified against the standard 18-parva division; `summary` is an editorial rendering, not a quotation.

passages.section: The dog at the gate of heaven
passages.speaker: Indra / Yudhishthira
events: Yudhishthira arrives at heaven
He refuses to enter while a dog that followed him is turned away
The dog is revealed as Dharma
passages.summary: At the gate, Yudhishthira is told the animal cannot come in. He refuses to abandon a creature that trusted him and stayed with him to the end, even at the cost of his own entry. Only then is the situation revealed for what it is. The passage is about what you owe a dependent when the arrangement stops being convenient.
passages.source_reference: Mahaprasthanika Parva — Yudhishthira and the dog at heaven's gate
passages.verification_note: Episode identity verified against the standard 18-parva division; `summary` is an editorial rendering, not a quotation.

passages.speaker: Yudhishthira / narrating voice
events: The five set out to walk north
Draupadi and then the others fall
Yudhishthira keeps walking
passages.summary: One by one the others drop from the road and Yudhishthira continues with a question he cannot answer. The narration does not tell him he is wrong to continue, and does not tell him he is right. It simply keeps walking with him.
passages.verification_note: Episode identity verified against the standard 18-parva division; `summary` is an editorial rendering, not a quotation.

passages.speaker: narrator
events: The clan turns on itself in a drunken quarrel
The survivors destroy one another
passages.summary: A whole people who cannot be killed by an enemy destroy each other over a trivial slight while drunk. The curse that produced it had been triggered by mocking a sage. The passage is a compressed lesson on how a grievance escalates once nobody is willing to be the one who stops it.
passages.source_reference: Mausala Parva — the destruction of the Yadavas
passages.verification_note: Episode identity verified against the standard 18-parva division; `summary` is an editorial rendering, not a quotation.

passages.speaker: Kunti
events: Kunti asks that rites be performed for her sons on both sides
Yudhishthira agrees
passages.summary: A mother who has lost sons on both sides asks the victor to perform the funeral rites for the defeated as well. The request is practical, unpaid-for and granted. It is the epic's earliest movement toward stopping the accounting and beginning the repair.
passages.source_reference: Stri Parva — Kunti's request for rites on both sides
passages.verification_note: Episode identity verified against the standard 18-parva division; `summary` is an editorial rendering, not a quotation.

passages.section: Sanjaya reports to the blind king
passages.speaker: Sanjaya
events: Sanjaya describes the war to the king who ordered it
He answers when asked whether the Pandavas can be defeated
passages.summary: A charioteer with sight is required to describe to a blind ruler exactly what his decision is producing, day after day, in detail he does not want. He answers honestly when asked whether his side can still win. The role is a study in delivering unwelcome information without softening it or dramatising it.
passages.source_reference: Udyoga Parva — Sanjaya's reports to Dhritarashtra
passages.verification_note: Episode identity verified against the standard 18-parva division; Sanjaya's narrated report continues through the war books, so no single chapter number is given.

passages.speaker: Bhishma
events: Yudhishthira asks what makes a true friend
Bhishma describes the qualities and the tests
passages.summary: Bhishma describes a friend as someone who tells you the truth, shares what they have, keeps what is entrusted to them, and stands by you in misfortune — and distinguishes this from the person who is agreeable while things go well. The definition is offered as a tool for choosing, not for comforting.
passages.verification_note: Theme is well attested across Bhishma's discourses; the exact section needs confirmation against the chosen edition before this passage may support a strong textual claim.

passages.section: Aranya Parva — the killing of a hunter by his own act
passages.speaker: narrator
events: A disguised enemy abducts the exiles
Bhima kills him
passages.summary: An enemy lives among the exiles under a false identity until he makes his move. The passage sits next to the text's many other tests of who is actually loyal and who only appears to be, and it makes the point that trust built on concealment cannot survive contact with the purpose it was built for.
passages.source_reference: Vana Parva — Aranya Parva, Jatasura's abduction
passages.verification_note: Episode identity verified against the standard 18-parva division; `summary` is an editorial rendering, not a quotation.

passages.section: Bhagavad Gita — the two paths of the mind (6.5 context)
passages.speaker: Krishna
events: Krishna distinguishes the self that lifts from the self that pulls down
passages.translation: For one who has conquered the mind, the mind is the best of friends; for one who has failed to do so, the mind will remain the greatest enemy.
passages.summary: A direct extension of the previous verse: the same faculty is either ally or adversary depending on what has been done with it. The burden is placed on cultivation rather than on temperament.
passages.verification_note: Verse reference verified against the standard Bhagavad Gita numbering; the English is a conventional rendering, not a scholarly translation, and no Sanskrit is quoted here.

passages.section: Krishna on the limits of forbearance
passages.speaker: Krishna
events: Krishna reviews every concession already made
He argues that forbearance has been exhausted
passages.summary: Krishna lists what has already been absorbed — the exile, the loss of kingdom, the humiliation — and argues that further restraint would not be virtue but complicity. The passage is the text's clearest counterweight to the idea that patience is always the higher course.
passages.source_reference: Udyoga Parva — Krishna on exhausted forbearance
passages.verification_note: Episode identity verified against the standard 18-parva division; `summary` is an editorial rendering, not a quotation.
